title: Schools, Study Houses, and Libraries in Jewish Drohiczyn
summary: The records show education as a sustained communal priority, spanning traditional study, modern schools, libraries, and teachers’ work.
editorialContent:
![The Bug River and Drohiczyn](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Drohiczyn_Zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_klasztorny_jezuit%C3%B3w_06.jpg/1920px-Drohiczyn_Zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_klasztorny_jezuit%C3%B3w_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)
## A town with several paths to learning

For Jewish children in Drohiczyn, education did not follow a single route. Religious study in the *heder*, study house, and yeshiva remained central, while modern schools brought general subjects and newer Jewish curricula to a wider range of pupils. Families also used Polish government schools, and some young people left town for further education. These paths overlapped, but they could also reflect real differences in religious outlook, language, and ideas about Jewish life.

The memorial book’s account is especially valuable for names, local institutions, and remembered disputes. It describes a long-standing religious elementary school and yeshiva, as well as schools that appeared in the late Russian imperial period and between the world wars. Its memories are not a complete census of pupils or teachers; they are a community’s retrospective record, preserved by survivors and contributors. What follows distinguishes that testimony from the broader context.

## Religious learning, from the study house to the yeshiva

The book describes elementary religious education and a yeshiva serving students from Drohiczyn and surrounding places. It dates the founding of a yeshiva for advanced study to 1905, and names Jacob Zamter and Aaron Kryvitsky among those associated with it. Its reference to a *heder* and yeshiva evokes different stages of learning: foundational instruction for children and more advanced study of Jewish texts. The account does not give a full institutional chronology, so the 1905 date should be understood as the book’s remembered starting point, not as an independently verified foundation record.

The changing arrangements after the First World War emerge unusually clearly in a 1923 letter reproduced in the memorial book. Rabbi Isaac Yaakov Kalenkovitch wrote of financial hardship, disagreements over whether the Talmud Torah should combine Torah and secular subjects, difficulty finding teachers, and poor families unable to pay tuition. He named more than fifty children whose parents could not afford the monthly fee. His letter also names educators and supporters, including Gavriel Kamenetsky, Moshe Aharon of Khomsk, and donors in the United States. It shows that the question was not simply whether to teach religiously, but how to fund teaching and who should determine the balance of subjects. [The letter and its editorial note](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/dro253.html) also distinguish the religious Talmud Torah from the later Tarbut-affiliated Moriah School.

A separate school, [Kehilat Yaakov Talmud Torah](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_5b3512b4d2923c3cabfc1d99), is remembered as founded in 1917 and expanded into a modern building in 1924. The record’s dates sit within a wider story of institutional change, but the supplied evidence does not establish that this was the same building or the same school arrangement described in every other account. The letters show how buildings, teachers, tuition, and ideological disagreements were closely bound together.

## Modern schools and competing visions

The memorial book records that a Jewish school received permission in 1883 and opened in 1885. Its surviving record names Isaac Rosenkrantz and Shlomo Shedrawitzky in connection with the school, but offers little detail about its curriculum or enrollment. It also recalls the [Yavne School](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_6ca739bc06e6761a9b4659fc), a modern Hebrew school that operated before the First World War and later closed. The book places newer schooling alongside, rather than simply in place of, traditional religious learning.

The best-documented interwar institution is [Moriah School](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_3402110e21280b3df03b6cfb). According to the memorial book, émigrés from Drohiczyn in America helped fund a school building after the First World War. Moriah taught a government-school-like general curriculum alongside Yiddish and Hebrew subjects and some Talmud. The book says the school was eventually taken over by the Tarbut movement; more religious families, dissatisfied with its direction, organized a separate Orthodox elementary school. The memoir does not present these institutions as interchangeable: they answered different expectations about what Jewish children should learn.

The wider record helps explain that distinction. Tarbut was part of a broader interwar network of Hebrew-language schools in Poland, supported by Zionist groups and combining Hebrew and Jewish history with secular subjects. Its presence in Drohiczyn connected a small-town school to a much wider educational movement, though the general history of Tarbut does not independently verify every local detail in the memorial book. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbut)) The book names [Moshe Bezdzheski](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_223beed1e8ba3b2ac8eefee8), [Asher Lishtsche](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_a3a041f9787bca135333e6a6), and [Betzalel Wolfson](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_00ca9dac0010219601f25301) among Moriah’s teachers. It also remembers [Naftali Shteynberg](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_421498b2e0290e48388889c1) and [Sender Shapira](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_2b63ab3c45f5ac9507212595) as educators in reformed religious schools or classes. Their biographies and roles suggest that access to learning depended not just on institutions, but on teachers able to carry knowledge across different educational settings.

## Libraries, public schooling, and the next step

Education extended beyond the classroom. The memorial book recalls a well-organized [Drohiczyn library](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_3db6fc4f628bb6b055768305) holding hundreds of books, founded by Tsvishvarts, and names S. Fishman as its chairman. A separate record describes a Hebrew-Russian library established around 1910, though its evidence begins with an OCR artifact and its exact relationship to the other library is uncertain. The [public library associated with Moriah](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_3402110e21280b3df03b6cfb) may likewise refer to a collection connected to the school rather than a wholly separate institution. The sources do not settle whether these were distinct libraries, changing names, or overlapping collections. Their presence nevertheless points to reading as a communal resource beyond formal lessons.

Some Jewish children attended the Polish government’s *Powszechna* school. According to the memorial book, many went there after Moriah to cover Polish subjects; others continued to gymnasia and then to teachers’ colleges or universities in [Pinsk](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_cfc750e3dd555e9abc6d7413), Brest, Vilna, or Warsaw. The book stresses that only a smaller share continued to higher education and that most children stayed at home. Its account therefore records both aspiration and constraint: local schooling widened access, but distance, finances, and family circumstances shaped how far students could go.

## What the school photographs cannot show

The memorial book’s school photographs and captions preserve names that a list of institutions alone would miss. A 1937 Moriah class caption identifies Levi Feldman among the pupils; the book also describes his later work as a teacher and director. Its biographical pages remember Wolfson as a respected educator and record the fate of teachers and pupils under Nazi persecution. These are the memorial book’s testimony, not a complete account of every student or survivor. The record does not establish the individual fates of all named pupils, and the absence of a name from these pages cannot establish what became of that person.

Outside sources consulted for this article add regional context, not an independent archive of Drohiczyn’s schools: YIVO’s Pinsk entry describes modern and postwar Jewish schooling in a nearby educational center, while the broader Tarbut record situates Moriah’s reported orientation in an interwar network. ([smtp.yivoencyclopedia.org](https://smtp.yivoencyclopedia.org/article/476?utm_source=openai)) No independent school register or archive specific to Drohiczyn’s institutions was located in the permitted sources. The memorial book’s account of the community’s schools therefore remains the principal evidence for their local histories. What it preserves is a varied educational landscape: religious study and modern curricula, local classrooms and distant colleges, teachers and librarians, and a persistent effort to make learning available despite poverty and disagreement.
